===================================================
Complete Empirical Research Plan
===================================================

---------------------------------------------------
1. Identification Strategy
---------------------------------------------------
Preferred design:  Difference-in-Differences (DiD) complemented by an event-study.

Why it fits  
•  The intervention (printing tax-inclusive prices) is introduced in a subset of stores and product groups at a discrete date, creating treated and untreated observations observed before and after the change.  
•  The panel structure (item × store × day/week) allows us to difference out permanent level differences across stores/items and common shocks across time.  
•  An event-study around the implementation date lets us visualize pre-trends, test for anticipation, and recover dynamic effects.

Alternative robustness designs (optional)  
•  Triple-difference: Use non-taxable items as an additional control dimension.  
•  Synthetic control at the store level if treatment is rolled out to only a few stores.  

---------------------------------------------------
2. Treatment and Control
---------------------------------------------------
Unit of observation: item i sold in store s on day/week t.

Treatment indicator  Treated_ist = 1 if the shelf/price tag for item i in store s shows the tax-inclusive price at time t; 0 otherwise.

Control group  All item-store-time observations that never (or not yet) display tax-inclusive prices. Two natural controls:
  (a) Same items in comparable stores that did not change tags.  
  (b) Untreated items in the same store (within-store control).

Treatment timing / event date  For each treated store (or aisle) record the first day price tags changed.  Define:
  Post_ist = 1{t ≥ implementation date of store s}.

Running variable & cutoff  Not applicable (not an RDD).

Sample window  e.g. 3 months pre and 3 months post, but keep a wider window for robustness.

---------------------------------------------------
3. Key Identifying Assumptions
---------------------------------------------------
A1. Parallel trends. In the absence of salient tags, treated and control observations would have followed the same time trend in demand.  
Plausibility: The chain sets uniform prices, so baseline trends in grocery demand are likely parallel; we will test in the event-study.

A2. No anticipation. Consumers did not change behavior **before** the tags were switched.  
Plausibility: Management did not publicize the experiment; tags were replaced overnight.

A3. Stable composition/SUTVA. The set of stores and products stays constant and there are no spill-overs (e.g., customers do not massively switch to neighboring stores).  
Plausibility: Most shoppers are local; we can test for traffic changes at neighboring stores.

A4. Exogeneity of treatment assignment. Stores/products chosen for the pilot were not selected because of trends in sales.  
Plausibility: Corporate HQ reports random or logistical allocation; we can document this and control for pre-period covariates.

---------------------------------------------------
4. Threats to Identification & Mitigations
---------------------------------------------------
T1. Differential price changes (manager discounts, promos) coincide with tag change.  
  • Mitigation: Include item × week fixed effects (captures any time-varying price common across stores); control for the posted **pre-tax** price in the regression.

T2. Store-level demand shocks (local events, renovations) correlate with roll-out.  
  • Mitigation: Add store × week fixed effects; perform leave-one-store-out robustness; verify event-study pre-trends.

T3. Consumer substitution across stores (treated to untreated).  
  • Mitigation: Focus on households with loyalty cards to assign a “home store”; re-estimate on shoppers that rarely shop elsewhere; check that total chain-wide demand for treated items falls.

---------------------------------------------------
5. R Code Outline
---------------------------------------------------
```r
#--------------------------------------------------
# 0. Packages
#--------------------------------------------------
library(data.table)     # fast data handling
library(fixest)         # high-dimensional FE regressions
library(did)            # Callaway–Sant’Anna optional
library(ggplot2)

#--------------------------------------------------
# 1. Load and clean data
#--------------------------------------------------
trans <- fread("grocery_transactions.csv")   # assume file has 1 row per item–store–day

# key variables assumed to exist:
# store_id, item_id, date, qty, pretax_price, posttax_price, tag_visible

# convert date to weekly panel
trans[, week := as.Date(cut(date, "week"))]

#--------------------------------------------------
# 2. Construct treatment indicators
#--------------------------------------------------
# Identify first week tags became visible per store–item
trans[, treat_start := min(week[tag_visible == 1]), by = .(store_id, item_id)]
trans[, treated := as.integer(tag_visible == 1)]                 # instantaneous
trans[, post  := as.integer(week >= treat_start)]                # persistent
trans[, did  := as.integer(post == 1)]                           # DiD dummy
# Keep balanced panel
setkey(trans, store_id, item_id, week)
trans <- trans[complete.cases(qty)]

#--------------------------------------------------
# 3. Main specification
# Y = log quantity; FE: store×week and item×week or store×item
#--------------------------------------------------
trans[, lqty := log1p(qty)]          # log(1+q)

est_main <- feols(lqty ~ did |
                    store_id^week + item_id^week,  # two-way time-varying FE
                  data = trans, cluster = ~store_id)

summary(est_main)

#--------------------------------------------------
# 4. Event-study for pre-trend test
#--------------------------------------------------
trans[, rel_week := as.integer(week - treat_start) / 7]   # weeks relative to start
# Keep a window [-12, +12]
es_data <- trans[rel_week >= -12 & rel_week <= 12]

est_es <- feols(lqty ~ i(rel_week, ref = -1) |
                  store_id + item_id + week,
                data = es_data, cluster = ~store_id)

iplot(est_es)    # pre-vs-post coefficients plot

#--------------------------------------------------
# 5. Robustness: triple-diff using non-taxable items
#--------------------------------------------------
trans[, taxable := as.integer(sales_tax > 0)]
est_tdd <- feols(lqty ~ did*taxable |
                   store_id^week + item_id^week,
                 data = trans, cluster = ~store_id)

summary(est_tdd)
```

---------------------------------------------------
6. Expected Results
---------------------------------------------------
Economic intuition suggests that higher tax salience makes the effective price more noticeable, decreasing demand.  
Prior on magnitude: For a typical combined state + local sales tax of 8%, fully internalized salience could reduce quantity by roughly the same elasticity response as an 8% price hike. With a short-run price elasticity of grocery demand of –0.7, we expect:

Δ log Q ≈ −0.7 × 0.08 ≈ −0.056  → about a 5–6 percent decline in quantity for treated items.

---------------------------------------------------
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (DiD)
(1 = clearly satisfied, 0 = questionable/absent)
---------------------------------------------------
C1. Parallel pre-trends………………………… 0.8  (will test with event study)  
C2. No anticipatory behavioral change……… 0.9  (overnight tag switch)  
C3. No spill-overs/Stable unit treatment…… 0.7  (possible cross-store shopping)  
C4. Consistent treatment classification……… 1.0 (direct observation of tags)  
C5. No simultaneous confounding shocks…… 0.7  (we control for price promos but cannot rule out all shocks)  

Average score ≈ 0.82 → overall credible but requires standard robustness work.

===================================================
